subject: PSHE and RSE (Islamic perspective)
source: National Curriculum / statutory RSHE guidance (Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education, Health Education); PSHE Association programme of study themes and KS3 mental health lessons (Drive PSHE folder); TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27, Careers Education and Guidance Policy and RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y5 lesson style. Qur'an and hadith references limited to well-known authenticated sources and cited plainly. RSE is taught from an Islamic perspective, to boys and girls separately; parents can see all RSE materials.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Respectful relationships and online safety
lessons.title: Healthy and unhealthy relationships: respect, boundaries and consent
objectives: Explain consent as freely given, informed and able to be withdrawn, in everyday situations
Recognise controlling behaviour and pressure in relationships
Link respect, modesty (haya) and dignity to healthy relationships and know where to get help

keywords.def: freely given agreement that can be withdrawn at any time
pressuring or forcing someone to do something
trying to dominate what another person does or feels
modesty and a sense of shame about what is wrong
the right to be respected and valued

starter: Bismillah. Name two features of a healthy friendship.
Give an assertive phrase for refusing something.

teach.heading: Healthy relationships
bullets: Respect, honesty, trust and equality
Both people have a voice
You feel safe and free to be yourself
Applies to family, friends and online contacts
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain that this lesson is about friendships, family and online contacts (in Islam, romantic relationships belong only within marriage), and is taught within the TGA RSHE Policy. Parents have been informed of the content. Revisit key features of healthy relationships. Link to Qur'an 30:21, which describes love and mercy between spouses as a sign from Allah, and to the hadith that the best of you are the best to their families (Tirmidhi). Link to RECIPE Integrity. Taught to boys and girls separately. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Consent in everyday life
bullets: Consent is a clear, free ‘yes’
Silence or fear is not consent
You can change your mind any time
Applies to touch, photos, secrets and belongings
teach.note: Begin with low-risk examples: borrowing a phone, hugging someone, taking and sharing a photo, reading private messages. Teach that consent must be freely given, informed and specific. Misconception: if someone did not say no, it is fine. Emphasise that we must stop and check if someone seems uncertain. Do not discuss sexual detail. Explain that the same principles apply in every relationship.

teach.heading: Pressure, coercion and control
bullets: Guilt-tripping, threats and bribes
Checking your phone or tracking you
Cutting you off from friends and family
Humiliation, jealousy and anger used to control
teach.note: Use invented case studies of friendships and online contacts rather than romantic ones. Examples: a friend threatens to share a secret if you don't do what they say; an older contact flatters a pupil and asks them to keep their chats secret. Ask pupils to identify the red flags. Explain that anyone can experience coercive behaviour, and it is never the victim's fault.

teach.heading: Values: haya, dignity and the law
bullets: Qur'an 24:30: lower the gaze and guard modesty
Hadith: modesty is part of faith
Everyone's dignity must be protected
UK law protects young people; the age of consent is 16
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 24:30 commands believers to lower their gaze and guard their modesty, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that modesty is part of faith (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain that Islamic teaching places intimate relationships within marriage, and that the law in the UK also sets an age of consent to protect young people. Keep to the facts; do not discuss details. If pupils ask questions, redirect to the question box and speak to the PSHE Lead.

teach.heading: Getting help
bullets: Tell a trusted adult or the DSL
Childline 0800 1111
NSPCC Helpline 0808 800 5000
In danger, call 999
teach.note: Make sure all pupils know the routes for help. Emphasise that no one will be blamed for reporting. Model what to say: ‘Something is happening that I'm not comfortable with and I need help.’ Explain that adults will take concerns seriously and act in the pupil's best interests. If a pupil discloses something during the lesson, follow safeguarding procedures and speak to the DSL the same day.

practice: Consent or not? (a) A friend says ‘ok’ after you keep asking five times. (b) A pupil says ‘yes, you can take the photo’ and later says ‘please delete it’. Explain each.
List three red flags of controlling behaviour.
Write two assertive sentences that set a boundary about sharing your phone.
independent: Write a short case study of an unhealthy friendship and how a pupil seeks help.
Create a poster: ‘Consent is…’ with five key points and a quotation from the lesson.
Write a paragraph explaining how haya and respect protect dignity.
exit: Name two places to get help.
lessons.homework: Talk with a trusted adult about what respect looks like in a family relationship and write four sentences about their view.
lessons.send: SEND: provide scenario cards with traffic-light responses and sentence frames. EAL: pre-teach ‘consent’, ‘coercion’ and ‘boundary’. Stretch: compare the idea of consent in UK law with Islamic ethical principles of respect and choice.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Respectful relationships and online safety
lessons.title: Sharing images and harmful content online
objectives: Explain the law and risks relating to nude or sexual images of under-18s
Describe how to respond to pressure, blackmail or harmful content and where to report
Evaluate misleading, extreme and sexually explicit content and why it is harmful

keywords.def: a nude or sexual image of a person
threatening to share something unless a person does what is demanded
false or misleading information
being drawn into extreme beliefs
a trust we must protect

starter: Bismillah. What is a digital footprint?
Name two places to report an online problem.

teach.heading: Online risks
bullets: Pressure to share images
Strangers and fake profiles
Unrealistic or harmful content
Extreme views and false news
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach this lesson factually, without graphic detail, in line with the TGA RSHE Policy and Online Safety and Acceptable Use Policy. Parents have been informed. Explain the aim: to prepare pupils so that they can protect themselves and others. Reassure pupils that no one will be blamed if they ask for help. Link to RECIPE Integrity and amanah. Taught to boys and girls separately. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Images and the law
bullets: It is illegal to take, share or keep nude images of under-18s
This includes images of yourself
Once sent, you lose control of it
Police focus on protecting young people
teach.note: State facts: in UK law a nude or sexual image of anyone under 18 is treated as an indecent image of a child. This applies even when a young person creates it themselves. The police have said they focus on safeguarding, not criminalising young people. Teach that images can be copied, shared and used to hurt. Link to the hadith that whoever conceals the fault of a Muslim, Allah will conceal him in this world and the next (Muslim).

teach.heading: Pressure and blackmail
bullets: Stop contact and do not send more
Do not pay, and do not delete evidence
It is never your fault
Tell a trusted adult; report to CEOP
teach.note: Explain that some people trick young people using fake profiles, flattery and then threats. Teach the steps: stop, save evidence, block, tell. Report Remove (Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation) can help get images taken down. Stress that adults will help without judgement. Role-play an invented chat in which a pupil receives pressure and chooses to tell an adult. Link to RECIPE Resilience.

teach.heading: Harmful content
bullets: Pornography presents a distorted picture
It can harm self-image and relationships
Extremist content uses emotion to recruit
Misinformation spreads fast: Qur'an 49:6
teach.note: Keep this brief and non-graphic. Explain that pornography is harmful and haram: it is unrealistic, can become a habit that is hard to break, and distorts how people see themselves and others; Qur'an 24:30-31 commands believers to lower their gaze. Anyone who has seen it should not feel trapped: close it, turn to Allah in repentance and talk to a trusted adult. Explain that extremist groups may target young people online with simple answers and a sense of belonging. Cite plainly: Qur'an 49:6, to verify information before acting on it. Teach lateral reading: check who made it and what other trusted sources say. Refer to the Prevent policy for concerns.

teach.heading: What to do
bullets: Close the page, do not share it
Talk to a trusted adult
Use parental controls and filters
Report to the DSL, platform, CEOP, Childline
teach.note: Summarise the key steps: close, tell, report. Explain that platforms have age restrictions and parents can set filters. Encourage pupils to build habits: ask whether it is true, kind and necessary before sharing. Close with a reminder that help is always available.

practice: True or false? (a) If you send a picture of yourself it cannot be illegal. (b) Blackmail is never your fault. (c) Report Remove can help get images taken down.
List the steps to take if someone pressures you to send a picture.
How can you check whether a shocking video is true?
independent: Create a flowchart: ‘I have received a worrying message — what do I do?’
Write a short dialogue showing a pupil telling a trusted adult about online pressure.
Write a paragraph on how amanah and haya protect us online.
exit: Why is it dangerous to share nude images of under-18s?
Give two steps to take if you are being blackmailed.
lessons.homework: Find out how to set up parental controls or filters on one device with a parent or carer, and write three sentences about what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: provide flowchart templates and visual steps. EAL: pre-teach legal vocabulary. Stretch: research how the Online Safety Act 2023 requires platforms to protect children.

lessons.title: Money matters: earning, budgeting and saving
objectives: Distinguish between needs and wants and create a simple budget
Explain saving, interest and the Islamic principle of avoiding riba
Recognise common scams and risks of debt

keywords.def: money coming in
money going out
a plan for income and spending
interest or increase on loans, forbidden in Islam
a trick to take your money or details

starter: Bismillah. Name two ways people earn money.
What is the difference between a need and a want?

teach.heading: Where money comes from
bullets: Pocket money, gifts and part-time work
Wages, salaries and self-employment
Benefits and student support
Earning halal income: Bukhari
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask: ‘How do people earn money?’ Explain that at 13 young people may do light part-time work, with limits on hours and types of work. Cite the hadith that no one has eaten better food than that which he eats from the work of his own hands (Bukhari). Link to RECIPE Integrity and Excellence. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Needs, wants and budgeting
bullets: Needs: food, shelter, clothing, safety
Wants: games, brands, treats
Budget: income minus spending
Save first, then spend
teach.note: Worked example: Zayd earns £30 a month from a weekend job. He saves £10, gives £3 as sadaqah and spends £17 on snacks and gaming credit. Ask: ‘What would you change?’ Show a budget table with income, savings, charity and spending. Misconception: a budget stops you having fun; it helps you plan for what matters. Link to RECIPE Contentment and Progress.

teach.heading: Saving and interest
bullets: Save for goals: short, medium, long term
Banks pay interest on savings
Interest on loans costs more over time
Qur'an 2:275: trade is lawful, riba forbidden
teach.note: Worked example: £100 at 5% simple interest earns £5 in a year. Borrowing £100 at 20% costs £20 in a year. Cite plainly: Qur'an 2:275, that Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba. Explain that Muslims seek halal ways of saving and borrowing. Islamic banks offer accounts and finance based on profit-sharing or buying and selling rather than interest. Pupils should discuss specific questions with family or a qualified scholar.

teach.heading: Giving and spending wisely
bullets: Zakat and sadaqah purify wealth
Qur'an 25:67: spend with moderation
Qur'an 17:26-27: do not waste
Hadith: we will be asked how we earned and spent
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 25:67 describes the servants of the Most Merciful as those who are neither extravagant nor stingy when they spend. Cite Qur'an 17:26-27 on waste. Cite the hadith that a person will be asked on the Day of Judgement about his wealth, how he earned it and how he spent it (Tirmidhi). Link to RECIPE Contentment.

teach.heading: Scams and risks
bullets: Too good to be true usually is
Never share bank details or codes
Beware of ‘get rich quick’ and gambling-style games
Ask an adult before spending online
teach.note: Show invented examples: a text offering a prize for a small fee; a social media post promising to double money; loot boxes in games. Teach the pause-and-check habit. Explain that debt can grow quickly. Mention Qur'an 83:1-3 as a warning against cheating in measure, relevant to fraud and fair dealing. Ask: ‘Who can you check with before spending or sharing details?’

practice: Zayd earns £30 a month. He saves £8, gives £2 to charity and spends the rest. How much does he spend?
£200 is saved at 3% simple interest for one year. How much interest is earned?
Which is a scam sign? (a) a prize you did not enter for (b) a bank letter you expected (c) a request to ‘act now’ and pay a small fee.
independent: Create your own monthly budget for £40 income including savings, charity and spending.
Write a leaflet: ‘Five tips for staying safe from scams’.
Explain in a paragraph how moderation and charity can be part of managing money.
exit: Name two signs of a scam.
lessons.homework: Make a savings plan for a goal costing £60: how much to save a week and for how long?
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-drawn budget table and use calculators. EAL: pre-teach finance vocabulary. Stretch: research how Islamic finance products such as murabaha work and summarise in your own words.

lessons.title: Careers and choices: strengths, options and pathways
objectives: Link strengths, interests and values to career sectors
Explain how choices at 14 and 16 affect later pathways
Challenge stereotypes and use reliable sources to research careers

keywords.def: a group of related jobs, such as health or technology
a route through education, training or work
a job with training that leads to a qualification
a fixed idea about a type of person
facts about jobs, pay and demand

starter: Bismillah. Name one job you would like to learn more about.

teach.heading: The world of work
bullets: Hundreds of careers across many sectors
Health, tech, law, engineering, education, creative
New jobs appear as technology changes
Skills matter: communication, problem-solving, teamwork
teach.note: Say bismillah. Refer to the TGA Careers Education and Guidance Policy. Ask pupils to name jobs in each sector and note that they probably know only a small share of what exists. Mention that the National Careers Service website has job profiles. Link to RECIPE Progress and Excellence. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Strengths, interests and values
bullets: What are you good at?
What do you enjoy?
What matters to you: service, faith, creativity?
Look for careers that match all three
teach.note: Ask pupils to draw a three-circle diagram with strengths, interests and values, and write one example in each. Discuss that work can be a way to serve others and earn halal provision. Cite plainly: Qur'an 62:10, which tells believers, after the prayer, to disperse in the land and seek Allah's bounty. Also cite the hadith that actions are judged by intentions (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask: ‘How can your future work benefit others?’

teach.heading: Choices at 14 and 16
bullets: GCSE choices keep doors open
Core subjects plus options
At 16: A levels, T levels, apprenticeships, college
In England you stay in education or training until 18
teach.note: Explain the pathways simply: A levels (academic), T levels (technical with industry placement), apprenticeships (earn while learning), and college courses. Point out that choices at 14 do not close every door but some careers need certain subjects, such as sciences for medicine. Encourage pupils to speak to subject teachers and the careers lead. Tell pupils that decisions can be changed.

teach.heading: Challenging stereotypes and barriers
bullets: Anyone can enter any career
Role models can inspire
Barriers: money, confidence, discrimination
Support: mentors, bursaries, advice
teach.note: Discuss gender and cultural stereotypes in careers, and examples of Muslim professionals in many fields. Avoid naming real people unless well known and appropriate. Ask: ‘What barriers might exist and how can we overcome them?’ Explain that discrimination in employment is unlawful under the Equality Act 2010. Link to RECIPE Resilience and Integrity: working with halal income and fairness.

teach.heading: Researching careers reliably
bullets: Use National Careers Service and gov.uk
Check pay and demand: labour market information
Talk to people in the job
Cross-check sources
teach.note: Show how to search for a job profile and what to look for: tasks, entry routes, hours, average pay, outlook. Teach pupils to compare at least two sources. Remind them that social media may glamorise or misrepresent jobs. Set the independent task. Close with a du'a to ask Allah for guidance and beneficial knowledge.

practice: Match the pathway: (a) learn on the job and earn (b) academic study in sixth form (c) technical course with work placement.
Name three strengths you have and one job where they might be useful.
Why is it important to check more than one source when researching a job?
independent: Research one career using the National Careers Service and complete a profile: tasks, qualifications, skills, pay, outlook.
Create a mind map of your strengths, interests and values with three possible careers.
Write a paragraph on how a halal career can be a way of serving others.
exit: Give one way to challenge a stereotype about careers.
lessons.homework: Interview someone about their job and write six sentences about what they do, what they enjoy and the skills needed.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a profile template and careers cards. EAL: use pictures for sectors. Stretch: compare two career pathways to the same job in detail.
